body: **Cameras on for the drills** — not the lectures

Analysts who do not identify themselves cause confusion that costs hours.
This session is recorded. The drills are your evidence.

slides.title: The Alert Pipeline
items: SENSORS — AV, firewall, WAF, DLP, EDR, NDR. Each one sees a slice.
SIEM — collects everything the sensors say, correlates it, ranks it.
ANALYST — you. The SIEM says 'interesting.' You decide if it is real.
ACTION — a ticket, an escalation, a phone call to a client at 2 AM.
RECORD — what you did and why. Six months later this is the only answer.

slides.title: The Tiers — Where You Sit
rows: Watch the queue, triage, verify, ticket, escalate
Investigate what L1 escalated, scope the incident
Hunt for what nobody alerted on, lead major incidents
Staffing, SLAs, client comms, containment decisions

slides.title: The Shift Handover — Five Sections
body: **Open items**  — tickets still in progress, with ticket number and state
**Escalated**  — what went to L2/L3, and who owns it now
**Watch items**  — not yet incidents, but they need eyes
**System status**  — anything down, degraded, or in maintenance
**Client notes**  — anything a client asked for or complained about
## The handover is the highest-risk moment in a SOC.
It is where information gets dropped — so it gets written down, and read back.

slides.title: The Read-Back Rule
body: ## Repeat the instruction in your own words before you act on it.
"So you want me to isolate WKS-042 — not WKS-024 — and notify the IT manager. Confirming."
## A good read-back contains three things:
The identifier, said back exactly — hostname, IP, ticket number
The action you are being asked to take
The notification — who you will tell
It takes four seconds. Pilots do it. Nurses do it. Analysts should do it.

slides.title: When to Stop and Ask
body: ## Three situations mean stop and seek clarification:
You do not understand the instruction
The instruction contradicts the SOP
Acting on it would exceed your authority
## Four questions you always have available:
"Can you repeat the hostname / IP / ticket number?"
"Now, or after I finish the current ticket?"
"That is above my authority — escalate, or are you authorising it?"
"The SOP says X and you are asking for Y. Which do I follow?"
**Asking is not weakness. Not asking is the error.**

slides.title: The Shift Huddle — 4 Minutes, On the Clock
items: Shift Lead opens and states the priorities for the shift.
Each member reports their open items — one sentence each.
The team agrees who picks up the watch item, by name.
Shift Lead closes with the single thing that cannot slip tonight.
In an office everyone stands, and that is what keeps it short. On a call, the timer does that job — and everyone speaks, every time.

slides.title: Lab Rules — and Your Desk Today
body: **No scanning, probing, or testing anything outside the lab network**
This applies from Day 1 to Day 15 — and after you graduate.

No live malware on any machine, ever

slides.title: The Afternoon Is Not a Half Day
body: **Tasks 5 and 6 carry the unit.**
Between them they are the whole of LO2 — perform workplace duties
following written notices. They are marked. If you run short of time,
those two are the ones that cannot slip.
**Task 3 is yours alone.** Write the handover from your own notes.
Leave a gap where you missed something and write "would confirm".
An honest gap is better work than a plausible guess.
**Task 5, Q1 is about a clock.** Almost everybody gets it wrong.
Read §3.3 twice. We open Day 2 with it.

slides.title: Reading an SOP: Watch the Verbs
rows: Expected. If you deviate, you must be able to justify it.
Your judgement — usually conditional on documenting it.
You have no authority. This is the edge of your role.
A clock is running. Know exactly when it starts.

left.head: ADVISORY
items: Tells you a threat, patch, or vulnerability exists
Usually informational, sometimes actionable
May change how you handle a detection type
Example: "7.4.2 gives false positives on signed binaries — verify manually before escalating"

right.head: CHANGE NOTICE
items: Tells you a system will be modified at a set time
Always relevant to your queue
Scheduled change is the #1 cause of false alerts
It tells you what is NOT covered just as much as what is

slides.title: Who Owns What on One Alert
Key Takeaways
items: A handover has five sections — and it is where information gets dropped
Read back the identifier, the action, and the notification
Three triggers to ask: don't understand, contradicts SOP, exceeds authority
shall = mandatory, should = justify, may = document, shall not = escalate
You are never Accountable for a containment decision
Keep every piece of evidence — it is your portfolio
The afternoon pack is due tonight. Tasks 5 and 6 are the ones that count.
